A new computer system built on top of pre-trained word vectors achieves excellent results on multiple sentence classification tasks. [P1_p1_c02] 
Computers struggle to understand the meaning of human language. [P1_p1_c03] 
Researchers tested a simple computer vision approach called a convolutional neural network on text tasks like sentiment analysis and question classification. [P1_p1_c02][P1_p1_c03] 
They used pre-trained word vectors, which are dense representations that place words with similar meanings close together in a vector space. [P1_p1_c03] 
This matters because language technology touches our daily lives through search queries and automated text analysis. [P1_p1_c03] 
The study shows that a simple computer model with little tuning performs remarkably well across different benchmarks. [P1_p1_c02][P1_p5_c04] 
Even a simple model using static vectors competes well against much more complex deep learning methods that require extra tools like parse trees. [P1_p4_c03] 
Pre-trained vectors act as good universal feature extractors that work well across different datasets. [P1_p4_c03] 
Furthermore, learning task-specific vectors through fine-tuning gives even better performance gains. [P1_p1_c02][P1_p4_c03] 
The researchers also proposed a simple modification to use both task-specific and static vectors at the same time. [P1_p1_c02] 
Overall, these models improved upon the previous state of the art on four out of seven tasks. [P1_p1_c02] 
These findings prove that unsupervised pre-training of word vectors is an important ingredient for teaching computers to process human language. [P1_p5_c04]
